theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before you start marking out a part, what should you check first?
options: The drawing or job sheet, for the sizes, material and number of parts
The cutting machine, to see which blade or disc is fitted today
The parts made on the last job, so that you can copy their sizes by eye
The scrap bin, to find a piece that looks about the right size

questions.stem: A drawing gives all sizes in millimetres. A length is shown as 1250. How long is the part in metres?
Why should a scriber have a cap or cork on its point when it is not being used?
options: To stop the point going rusty in the damp sea air
To protect people from stab cuts and keep the point sharp
To stop the scriber rolling off the bench onto the floor
To stop marking blue drying hard on the hardened point

questions.stem: The head of a centre punch has spread out and cracked (a "mushroom" head). What should you do?
options: Use it with a lighter hammer so the head does not crack more
Wrap the head with tape so that it is easier to hit cleanly
Keep using it, because a wider head is easier to strike
Stop using it until the head is ground back to shape

questions.stem: Which item of PPE is most important when you strike a centre punch with a hammer?
options: Ear muffs
Safety glasses
A dust mask
A welding apron

questions.stem: Which tool is used to scratch a fine, clear line on bright steel?
options: Scriber
Centre punch
Try square
Steel rule

questions.stem: Which tool would you use to mark a line at 90° to a straight edge of a steel plate?
options: Dividers
Odd-leg calipers
Centre punch
Try square

questions.stem: Which tool is best for scribing a circle 80 mm across on a steel plate?
options: A scriber and a steel rule
A steel tape measure
Dividers
Odd-leg calipers

questions.stem: Odd-leg calipers (also called jenny calipers) are mainly used to…
options: scribe a line parallel to the edge of a piece of metal
measure the thickness of a sheet to the nearest 0.01 mm
check that a corner is square before it is welded
make a deep dent so that a drill point does not wander

questions.stem: You are marking dark, hot-rolled steel that will be cut with a gas torch. Which marker stays visible best when the metal gets hot?
options: Lead pencil
Felt-tip marker
Wax crayon
Soapstone

questions.stem: An electrician must mark a straight line about 6 m long along a wall for a cable trunking run. Which tool is quickest for this?
options: A 300 mm steel rule moved along the wall step by step
A try square held against the edge of the ceiling
A chalk line, set level and snapped on the wall
A pair of dividers stepped along the wall

questions.stem: How can you check that a try square is still accurate?
options: Check that the stock and the blade are both free of rust
Mark a line, flip the square over, mark again: the lines should match
Measure the blade length and the stock length with a tape
Tap it gently on the edge of the bench and listen for a clear ringing sound

questions.stem: The hook on the end of a steel tape measure is loose and slides a little. Why is it made like this?
options: It is worn out and the whole tape should be thrown away
It was made badly, so every reading will be slightly wrong
It lets the blade bend round corners without kinking
It moves by its own thickness for inside and outside measuring

questions.stem: To read a steel rule accurately, where should your eye be?
options: Straight above the mark you are reading
Low down, looking along the rule from one end
To one side, so your shadow does not fall on it
Far back, so you can see the whole rule at once

questions.stem: What is a datum when marking out?
options: The last line you mark, used to check all the others
The type of metal written in the title block
An edge or line that all sizes are measured from
A small dot made by a prick punch on a line

questions.stem: Why is it better to measure every hole position from one datum edge, rather than from the hole before it?
options: It is quicker because you only need a short rule
Small errors do not add up from one hole to the next
The holes will come out larger and easier to fit
It means you do not need to check the drawing

questions.stem: Why is marking blue (layout dye) put on a steel surface before marking out?
options: So that scribed lines show up clearly
So that the steel does not rust later
So that the scriber point stays sharp
So that the punch marks go in deeper

questions.stem: What should you do to the steel before you put on marking blue?
options: Heat it with a torch so that the dye dries quickly
Wipe it with oil so that the dye spreads evenly
Clean off dirt, grease and loose rust
Paint it white so that the dye shows up better

questions.stem: What is the main use of a centre punch?
options: To mark scribed lines with very light dots
To cut small round holes in thin sheet metal
To stamp the part number or job number on the finished work
To make a dent so a drill starts in the right spot

questions.stem: Why are small punch marks (witness marks) put along a scribed cutting line?
options: To make the metal easier to bend along the line
So the line can still be seen if the blue rubs off
So that the cutting disc follows the dents by itself
To show the inspector how many cuts are needed

questions.stem: What is the right way to use a centre punch?
options: Hold it at a slant and hit it several times, hard
Hold it upright and hit it as hard as you can, once
Tilt it to find the mark, stand it upright, then tap it
Hold it loosely by the tip and strike it with a mallet

questions.stem: You need to scribe a circle of 120 mm diameter with dividers. What should the dividers be set to?
options: 60 mm
120 mm
240 mm
30 mm

questions.stem: Which part of a combination set is used to find the centre of the end of a round bar?
options: The square head
The centre head
The protractor head
The spirit level

questions.stem: Before you scribe a circle with dividers, what should be at its centre?
options: A dab of oil so that the leg can turn freely
A cross scribed with the point of the dividers
A small hole drilled right through the plate
A light punch mark for the divider leg to sit in

questions.stem: Which tool lets you mark a line at 30° to a straight edge?
options: Try square
Odd-leg calipers
Steel rule
Protractor

questions.stem: The square head of a combination set can be used to mark lines at which two angles?
What is a surface plate used for in marking out?
options: A flat reference surface to set up and mark the work on
A heavy steel plate to hammer bent bars and strips straight on
A steel table for welding small parts together
A hot plate for drying marking blue quickly

questions.stem: A surface gauge (scribing block) is used on a surface plate to…
options: measure how hard the work piece is
hold round bar while it is punched
scribe lines at a set height above the plate
check that the plate is level with the floor

questions.stem: What are vee blocks used for when marking out?
options: To bend thin strips of metal into a vee shape
To hold round bar steady while it is marked
To raise flat plate so that it can be cut below
To measure the angle of a chamfered edge

questions.stem: When you cut along a marked line, on which side of the line should the cut be made?
options: Right on the centre of the line every time
On the side of the part that you are keeping
On whichever side is easier to reach
On the waste side, so the part keeps its size

questions.stem: Why do workers often mark the waste part of the metal with a cross or hatching lines?
options: So nobody cuts on the wrong side of the line
So the scrap can be sold at a higher price
So the steel does not rust where it is marked
So the inspector can count how many parts there are

questions.stem: Before drilling into a wall to fix a box or bracket you have marked, what should you do?
options: Wet the wall so that the drill bit stays cool
Mark the spot again with a thicker pen
Check for hidden cables and pipes with a detector
Drill a small test hole somewhere else first

questions.stem: Shanique is marking the height of several switch boxes along a wall in a house in May Pen. What should all the heights be measured from?
options: The ceiling, because it is always level
The top of the nearest window frame
One agreed level datum line on the wall
The bottom of each box already fitted

questions.stem: Which tool uses a weight hanging on a string to show a true vertical line on a wall?
options: Plumb bob
Chalk line
Try square
Trammel

questions.stem: A team sets out a large rectangle on the floor. One side is 3 m and the other is 4 m. If the corner is square, the diagonal will measure…
options: 7 m
6 m
5 m

questions.stem: You have marked out a rectangle on a steel sheet. A quick way to check that its corners are square is to…
options: measure all four sides and add them together
measure both diagonals and check they are equal
look at it from the other side of the workshop
check that the edges of the sheet are straight

questions.stem: Some sites use a laser level to mark lines on walls. What is the main safety rule?
options: Never look into the beam or point it at anyone's eyes
Only use it outdoors when the sun is shining
Leave it switched on overnight so it stays accurate
Wear ear muffs the whole time the laser is running

questions.stem: When you finish marking out a part, what is the best check?
options: Ask the next worker to cut it and see if it fits
Compare it roughly with a part made last week
Check that the lines are dark enough to see
Measure every size again against the drawing

questions.stem: Some older drawings and tools use inches. How many millimetres are there in 1 inch?
options: 10 mm

questions.stem: The same shape must be marked out on 20 pieces of sheet. What is a good method?
options: Mark each piece freehand by eye to save time
Mark one piece, cut it, then trace round each new piece in turn
Make and check one accurate template, then mark round it
Mark all 20 pieces from offcuts left over from the last job

questions.stem: Damp, salty air in Jamaica can make tools rust. How should marking out tools be stored?
options: In a bucket of water so that they stay clean
Clean, lightly oiled and kept in a box or rack
Loose in the bottom of a tool bag with other tools
Outside in the sun so that they stay dry

questions.stem: Why should a try square or steel rule never be used as a lever or a hammer?
options: It will leave marks on the top of the bench
It will lose its coat of marking blue
It will become too sharp to handle safely
It may bend and stop being accurate

questions.stem: A scriber point has gone blunt. What will happen to the lines you mark with it?
options: They will be thinner and harder to see
They will be deeper and more accurate
They will be wide and less accurate
They will not need any marking blue

questions.stem: At the end of the job you find that the steel rule has a bent end. What should you do?
options: Report it and label it so that it is repaired or replaced
Put it back quietly so that you are not blamed
Straighten it with a hammer and keep using it
Cut off the bent end and carry on using the rest of the rule as normal

questions.stem: Before marking out, you check that the plate you were given is the right material. Where on the drawing would you look?
options: On the label of the marking blue tin
In the title block or the notes
On the back of the supplier's invoice
By the weight of the plate when lifted

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan and prepare before marking out a steel bracket from a drawing.
essays.modelAnswer: First I read the drawing and the job sheet. I check that it is the latest revision, and note the sizes, the material, the thickness and how many parts are needed. If anything is unclear I ask my supervisor before I start. Next I get the right material and check its size and condition. I plan where the parts will go on the plate so that there is little waste, and so that I can use a straight, clean edge as my datum. I collect the tools I need, such as a scriber, steel rule, try square, dividers and punches, and check that they are clean, sharp and not damaged. I clean the plate, file off any burrs on the datum edges, and put on a thin, even coat of marking blue so that my lines will show clearly.
markingPoints: Reads the drawing and job sheet, checks the revision, sizes, material and quantity
Gets and checks the correct material
Plans the layout to reduce waste and chooses straight datum edges
Collects the right tools and checks their condition
Cleans and deburrs the surface and applies marking blue

essays.stem: Explain the main hazards when marking out in a workshop or on site, and how each one is controlled.
essays.modelAnswer: Scriber and divider points are sharp and can stab or cut, so I keep caps on them and never carry them in a pocket. Chips can fly when I strike a punch, so I wear safety glasses, and I do not use a punch with a mushroom head. Cut steel has sharp edges and burrs, so I file them off and wear gloves when I handle plate. Steel sheets are heavy, so I lift with my legs and get help for large sheets. Marking blue gives off fumes and can catch fire, so I use it where there is good air flow, keep the lid on and keep it away from sparks and flames. On site, I check walls for hidden cables and pipes before drilling, and I never look into the beam of a laser level. I follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Sharp points of scribers and dividers: caps, careful carrying
Flying chips from punching: safety glasses, no mushroom heads
Sharp edges and heavy sheet: deburr, gloves, safe lifting
Marking blue: ventilation, lid on, away from heat and sparks
On site: check for hidden cables or pipes, laser beam safety

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you would mark out and punch the positions of four holes on a steel plate from a drawing.
essays.modelAnswer: I clean the plate, remove the burrs from the datum edges and put on a thin coat of marking blue. I check the two datum edges on the drawing. Using a steel rule and odd-leg calipers, or a try square and scriber, I measure each hole centre from the datum edges and scribe two thin lines that cross at each centre. I measure every position from the datums, not from the hole before, so that errors do not add up. I check all the sizes against the drawing again. Then I make a light mark with a prick punch exactly where the lines cross, and check it with a magnifier or by eye. When it is right, I deepen it with a centre punch, tilting the punch to find the mark and then standing it upright before tapping it. I can scribe a circle the size of each hole with dividers to show the drill size.
markingPoints: Cleans, deburrs and applies marking blue
Measures each centre from the datum edges and scribes crossing lines
Checks the positions against the drawing before punching
Prick punches first, then centre punches correctly (tilt, upright, tap)
Marks the hole size with dividers or checks the finished marks

essays.stem: Describe how you would mark out the positions of three switch or socket boxes and a straight horizontal trunking run on a wall in a building.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the drawing or layout to find where the boxes and the trunking must go and at what height. I agree a level datum line with my supervisor, measured from the finished floor level, and I mark it lightly on the wall with a spirit level and pencil. I measure the height of each box from this datum line, not from the ceiling or a window, because they may not be level. I use the spirit level or a plumb bob to make the sides of each box vertical, and I draw round a box or template. For the trunking run, I mark both ends at the correct height, then snap a chalk line between them and check it with the level. Before drilling, I check the wall with a cable and pipe detector. Finally I measure everything again against the drawing.
markingPoints: Reads the layout drawing for positions and heights
Sets a level datum line and measures all heights from it
Uses a level or plumb bob for vertical and horizontal lines
Uses a chalk line for the long trunking run and checks it
Checks for hidden cables and pipes, and re-checks against the drawing

essays.stem: Compare marking out on steel plate in the workshop with marking out on a wall or floor on site. Say how the tools and methods differ.
essays.modelAnswer: In the workshop the work is usually small enough to put on a bench or surface plate. The surface is cleaned and coated with marking blue, and fine lines are scratched with a scriber, using a steel rule, try square, dividers and odd-leg calipers. Hole centres are punched. The accuracy is high, often to a fraction of a millimetre. On site, the surfaces are large, such as walls, ceilings and floors, and you cannot scratch them, so you mark with a pencil, chalk or marker. Long lines are made with a chalk line or a laser level, and a spirit level and plumb bob are used to get lines level and vertical. Sizes are measured with a long tape from a datum line or the finished floor level. On site you must also check for hidden cables and pipes, and think about working at height and other people around you.
markingPoints: Workshop: bench or surface plate, marking blue and scribed lines
Workshop: fine tools such as rule, square, dividers, calipers and punches; high accuracy
Site: pencil, chalk or marker on large surfaces; tape from a datum or floor level
Site: chalk line, laser, spirit level and plumb bob for long, level and vertical lines
Site: extra hazards such as hidden services, height and other people

essays.stem: Explain the common causes of mistakes in marking out and how a careful worker avoids them.
essays.modelAnswer: One cause is working from an old drawing, so I always check the revision. Another is measuring each size from the last mark instead of from a datum, which lets small errors add up; I measure from one datum edge. Reading a rule from an angle gives a wrong reading, so I look straight down at the mark. A blunt scriber makes thick lines that are hard to follow, so I keep it sharp. A rule with a worn or bent end, or a tape with a damaged hook, reads wrong, so I check my tools and report damaged ones. A square that is out of true gives lines that are not at 90°, so I check it. Rushing also causes mistakes, so I measure twice, check every size against the drawing at the end, and ask someone to check important work.
markingPoints: Wrong or old drawing: check the revision and the sizes
Errors adding up: measure from one datum
Reading from an angle: eye straight over the mark
Blunt or damaged tools (scriber, rule end, tape hook, square): check and replace
Rushing: measure twice and check the finished marking against the drawing

essays.stem: Describe how you should care for and store marking out tools so that they stay accurate and safe to use.
essays.modelAnswer: After use I wipe each tool clean of dirt, chalk and marking blue. Because the air in Jamaica is warm, damp and often salty, I put a thin film of light oil on steel tools to stop rust. I store rules, squares and dividers in a box, drawer or rack where they cannot be dropped or have heavy tools thrown on them, because a small knock can spoil their accuracy. I keep caps on scriber and divider points. I never use a rule as a screwdriver or a square as a hammer. I keep a tape measure closed and dry, and do not let the blade snap back. Punches with mushroom heads are ground back to shape, and blunt scribers and punches are sharpened by a competent person. Any tool that is damaged or no longer accurate is labelled and reported so that it is repaired or replaced.
markingPoints: Cleans tools after use
Light oil to prevent rust in damp, salty air
Stores in a box or rack so that tools are not dropped or knocked
Caps on points; tools used only for their proper job
Dresses or sharpens worn tools; labels and reports damaged tools

essays.stem: Explain how you would choose a marking method for different surfaces: bright mild steel, black steel that will be flame cut, galvanised or aluminium sheet, and a painted wall.
essays.modelAnswer: On bright mild steel I put on marking blue and scratch fine lines with a scriber, because this gives the most accurate lines. On black hot-rolled steel that will be flame cut or welded, a scratched line is hard to see and ink burns off, so I use soapstone or a metal-marking pencil, and I can add centre punch marks along the line. On galvanised sheet, a scratch cuts through the zinc coating and lets rust start, and on aluminium a deep scratch on a bend line can start a crack, so I use a sharp pencil or a fine marker instead, unless the line is on the waste side. On a painted wall I use a pencil or chalk, because a scratch or ink would spoil the finish, and I mark lightly so that the marks can be wiped off later.
markingPoints: Bright steel: marking blue and a scriber for fine lines
Black steel for flame cutting or welding: soapstone or a metal-marking pencil, with punch marks
Galvanised: avoid scratching through the coating (pencil or marker)
Aluminium: avoid scratches on bend lines (pencil or marker)
Painted wall: pencil or chalk, marked lightly so that it can be removed

essays.stem: Describe how you would check a finished marking out before the part is cut or drilled, and what you would do if you found a mistake.
essays.modelAnswer: I put the drawing beside the work and check every size again, measuring from the same datum edges that I used for marking. I check that the lines are fine and clear, that hole centres are punched where the lines cross, and that the hole sizes and the number of holes are right. On rectangles I measure both diagonals to see that they are equal, and I check angles with a square or protractor. I check that the waste side of each cutting line is marked. For important work I ask another person or my supervisor to check it too. If I find a mistake, I clean off the wrong marks, put on fresh marking blue and mark that part again. If a wrong punch mark cannot be removed, or the material is spoiled, I tell my supervisor before going on.
markingPoints: Re-measures every size from the datums against the drawing
Checks lines, punch marks, hole sizes and the number of features
Checks square with diagonals and angles with a square or protractor
Has important work checked by a second person
Corrects mistakes by re-blueing and re-marking, and reports spoiled material

essays.stem: Describe what you should do at the end of a marking out job, before you leave the work area.
essays.modelAnswer: I check that the marked parts are complete and label them with the job number or part name, so that the next person knows what they are and which way up they go. I hand them over, or put them where my supervisor tells me. I put the lid back on the marking blue and store it away from heat and sparks, because it can catch fire. Rags with dye or solvent on them go in the correct closed metal bin. I clean my tools, oil the steel ones lightly and put them back in their box or rack, with caps on the points. I sweep up filings and offcuts and put scrap in the scrap bin. If any tool is damaged or any material is short or spoiled, I report it to my supervisor and write it on the job sheet if one is used.
markingPoints: Labels and hands over the marked parts
Closes and stores marking blue safely; disposes of dirty rags correctly
Cleans, oils and stores tools, with caps on points
Cleans the area and puts scrap in the right place
Reports damaged tools or material problems and records them

practical1.title: Mark out and punch a steel template plate from a drawing
practical1.brief: As a group, read the drawing the assessor gives you and plan the job together. Each member then marks out one steel template plate (about 150 mm × 100 mm × 3 mm) with two datum edges, a 45° chamfer line on one corner, four hole centres, one 50 mm diameter circle and the outline of a slot. Every member cleans and deburrs their own plate, puts on marking blue, scribes the lines, prick punches and then centre punches the hole centres, and scribes the circle with dividers. When the plates are finished, members swap plates and check each other's work against the drawing, writing the sizes they measure on a check sheet. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when every plate is checked and the area is clean.
materials: 1 mild steel plate per member, about 150 mm × 100 mm × 3 mm, cut square
The drawing of the template plate and a check sheet
Marking blue (layout dye) and clean rags
Scribers, 300 mm steel rules and try squares or combination sets
Prick punches, centre punches and ball pein hammers
photos: The group reading the drawing, with the datum edges marked on it
Each plate cleaned, deburred and coated with marking blue
Lines, chamfer and hole centres scribed on a plate
Hole centres punched and the circle scribed with dividers
A finished plate with a steel rule beside it showing a key size
Members checking each other's plates, with the check sheet
Tools cleaned and put away, and the bench clear
checklist: Read the drawing and named the two datum edges before starting
Checked the tools before use (scriber sharp, square true, punch heads sound)
Cleaned and deburred the plate and applied a thin, even coat of marking blue
Measured every feature from the datum edges and scribed fine, clear lines
Prick punched, then centre punched exactly on the line crossings
Scribed the circle with dividers set to the correct radius
Finished sizes within the tolerance set by the assessor
Checked another member's plate and recorded the sizes on the check sheet
Wore safety glasses when punching and filing, and left tools clean and stored
safety: Wear safety glasses when punching and filing
Keep caps on scribers and dividers when they are not in your hand
Deburr sharp edges and wear gloves when handling plate
Do not use a punch with a mushroom head
Marking blue can catch fire: use it with good air flow, keep the lid on and keep it away from heat and sparks

practical2.title: Set out fixing positions on a practice wall board and a square rectangle on the floor
practical2.brief: As a group, use the layout sketch the assessor gives you to set out work on the Centre's practice wall board and on the workshop floor. On the board, mark a level datum line, then mark the outlines of two electrical boxes and one steel shelf bracket at the heights and spacing on the sketch, a vertical line using a plumb bob, and a horizontal trunking or conduit run using a chalk line. On the floor, set out a rectangle 1.5 m × 2 m with masking tape, using the 3-4-5 method to make the first corner square, and check that the two diagonals are equal. Share the roles (holding the tape, marking, levelling, checking) and swap them, so that every member marks at least one item and checks at least one item. All marks must be within reach from the floor: do not climb. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the work is checked and the area is clean.
materials: The Centre's practice wall board and the layout sketch
A spirit level (600 mm or longer) and a plumb bob
Pencils and a small try square
An electrical box or box template, and a bracket template
A record sheet for the measured sizes
photos: The datum line on the board, with the spirit level on it showing the bubble centred
The plumb bob hanging beside the marked vertical line
Box and bracket outlines with their heights written beside them
The chalk line snapped for the trunking or conduit run
The floor rectangle with tapes showing both diagonals
The group checking the marks against the sketch, and the area cleared
checklist: Read the sketch and agreed the datum line with the group
Set the datum line level, checking the spirit level both ways round
Measured box and bracket positions from the datum, not from the ceiling
Used the plumb bob or level correctly for the vertical line
Snapped a tight, straight chalk line and checked it with the level
Set out the floor corner with the 3-4-5 method and checked the diagonals
Took a fair share of the roles and called out measurements clearly
Recorded the measured sizes and cleaned up the chalk and tape at the end
safety: Keep all marks within reach from the floor; do not climb on chairs or benches
Keep tapes and chalk lines out of walkways while they are stretched out
Do not let a steel tape snap back; its edge can cut
Do not drill into the board or wall during this task
